script.title: Why the Canal Needed a Disease War

lines: A colonel set pans of sulfur alight in every building in Panama.
The French had tried to dig a canal here first.
Yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers.
By 1884, the death rate was over 200 per month.
Doctors had blamed yellow fever on filth, and malaria on bad vapors.
But between 1897 and 1902, both diseases were shown to be spread by mosquitoes.
In 1904, the United States took over.
William Gorgas became head of sanitation.
Inspectors searched houses for mosquito larvae.
Carpenters removed anything where still water could collect.
You see, it's like a bucket of rainwater left in your yard.
Leave it, and it fills with wriggling bugs.
Mosquito larvae live just below the surface of standing water.
Workers sprayed oil on the pools to destroy them.
Every building was fumigated, using up the entire US supply of sulfur and pyrethrum.
The commission's head asked President Roosevelt to remove Gorgas for his costly obsession with mosquitoes.
Roosevelt was told he would get his canal if he supported Gorgas.
In 1906, only one case of yellow fever was reported.
But black workers, most of the workforce, still died at ten times the rate of white workers.
Many lived in tents outside the mosquito-controlled zone.

claims.claim: Gorgas fumigated residences: pans of sulfur or pyrethrum were placed in the rooms, sprinkled with wood-alcohol and set alight; fumigation was extended to all of Panama and every building was fumigated, using up the entire US supply of sulfur and pyrethrum.
The French tried to build the Panama Canal; yellow fever, malaria and other tropical diseases killed thousands of workers; by 1884 the death rate was over 200 per month.
Traditionally yellow fever had been thought to be caused by contact with filth and malaria by noxious vapors; between 1897 and 1902 both diseases were shown to be spread by mosquitoes.

The United States took control of the Panama Canal project in 1904; Colonel William Crawford Gorgas was appointed head of hospitals and sanitation; inspectors searched houses and buildings for mosquito larvae, and carpenters eliminated places where stagnant water could collect.
Mosquito larvae live just below the surface of standing water; workers with spray tanks sprayed oil on standing pools, so the larvae could be destroyed.

Theodore P. Shonts, head of the commission, asked President Roosevelt to remove Gorgas because of his costly obsession with mosquitoes; Roosevelt was told he would get his canal if he supported Gorgas.
In 1906, only one case of yellow fever was reported.
Black workers, the majority of the canal workforce, continued to die at ten times the rate of white workers in 1906; many had to live in tents and tenements outside the mosquito-controlled zone.

cast.gorgas: a 50 year old American army doctor, tall and slim, a neat white moustache, thinning white hair, kind blue eyes, a white tropical army uniform with a high collar and brass buttons, 1900s
cast.olddoctor: a 65 year old French doctor, short and plump, a bushy white beard, a bald pink head, a black frock coat and a black top hat in his hand, 1880s
cast.inspector: a 30 year old Panamanian sanitation inspector, lean, light brown skin, a thin black moustache, a wide white straw hat, a khaki shirt with rolled sleeves, 1900s
cast.worker: a 25 year old Black Caribbean canal worker, tall and muscular, a shaved head, a sweat-soaked faded blue cotton shirt and brown work trousers, 1900s
cast.shonts: a 49 year old American businessman, heavy build, dark hair slicked and parted in the middle, a clean-shaven fleshy face, a light grey suit with a white waistcoat, 1900s
cast.roosevelt: a 47 year old American president, stocky and broad-chested, small pince-nez glasses on a black cord, a bushy brown moustache, a wide toothy grin, short brown hair, a black frock coat, 1900s
